question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Guducyadi Varga, Chapter 3, verse 284):

से का अथ लड्डेश्वरो मानी रावणो राक्षसाधिषः । रामपत्नी बलात्सीतां जहार मदनातुरः ।।१।। ततस्त बलवान् रामो रिपुं जायाऽपहारिणम् । वृतो वानरसैन्येन जघान रणमूर्धनि ।। १।। हते तस्मिन्सुरारातौ रावणे बलगर्विते । देवराजः सहस्राक्षः परितुष्टश्चराघवे ।।३।। तत्र ये वानराः केचिद्राक्षसैर्निहता रणो । तानिन्द्रो जीवयामास संसिच्यामृतवृष्टिभिः ।।४।। ततो येषु प्रदेशेषु कपिगात्रात्परिच्युताः । पीयूषबिन्दवः पेतुस्तेभ्यो जाता गुडूचिका ।।५।। गुडूची मधुपर्णी स्यादमृताऽमृतवलरी । छिन्नाछिन्नरुहा छिन्नोद्धवा वत्सादनीति चं ।।६।। जीवन्ती तन्त्रिका सोमा सोमवली च कुण्डली । चक्रलक्षणिका धीरा विशल्या च रसायनी ।।७।। चन्द्रहासा वयस्था च मण्डली देवनिर्मिता । गुड्डची कटुका तिक्ता स्वादुपाका रसायनी ।।८।। संग्राहिणी कषायोष्णा लघ्वी बल्याऽग्निदीपिनी । दोषत्रयामतृड्दाहमेहकासांश्च पाण्डुताम् ।।९।। कामलाकुष्ठवातास्त्रज्वरक्रिमिवमीन्हरेत् । (प्रमेहश्वासकासार्शः कृच्छ्रह्रद्वोगवातनुत्) ।।१०।।
answer_text: GUDÜCYÄDI VARGA GUDÜCĪ Latin: Tinospora cordifolia, (willd.) Miers Fam: Menispermaceae Hin: Giloya Eng: Tinospora Once upon a time a king of demon Rāvaṇa forcefully taken away Lord sita, the wife of Lord Ram. Then there was a war between Rāmā and Rāvaṇa, durning this war Rāmā killed Ravana. The Lord Rāmā made a special prayer to Lord Indra as to resurrect all the Vānaras (Monkeys) and bear from his army that had died durning the war with the demon Ravana. Once hearing this wish from Lord Rama, Lord Indra sprinkled nectar from the hevan to resurrect the Vānar (Monkeys), as the nectar drops fell upon the bodies of died Vānaras (Monkeys), they suddenly come back to life, few drops of nectar fell on the ground from the sacred Gudūcī plants. Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): Madhu parṇi, Amṛtā, Amṛtāvallarī, Chinnā, Chinnaruhā, Chinnōdbhavā, Vatsādanī, Jīvantī, Tantrikā, Somā, Somavallī, Kuṇdalī, Cakralakṣaṇikā, Dhīrā, Viṣalyā, Rasayanī, Candrahāsā, Vayasthā, Maṇḍalī and Devanirmitā. Guṇa karma (Properties and indications): Gudūcī is Kaṭu (Pungent), Tikta (Bitter) and Kaşāya (Astringent) in taste, Madhura (Sweet) in post digestion, Rāsayana (Aphrodisiac), Grahī (Absorbent), Uṣṇavīrya (Hot in potency), Laghu (Light for digestion), Balyā (Promoters strength), Dīpana (Appetizers) and subsides all Tridoṣas. It is useful in diseases like Ama (Undigested food), Tṛṣnā (Thrist), Dāha (Burning sensation), Prameha (Diabetes), Kāsa (Cough), Pāṇḍu (Anemia), Kāmala (Jaundice), Kuṣṭa (Leprosy), Vātarakta (Gout), Jvara (Fever), Krmi (Worm infestations) and Vāmi (Vomiting). It is also useful in Prameha (All twenty types of Prameha), Swāsa (Dysponea), Kāsa (Cough), Arśas (Piles), Mūtrakrcchra (Dysuria) and Hrudroga (Cardiac diseases). Note: Stems of Tinospora malbarica and T. crispa are the common adulterants. Utpattisthāna (Natural territory): Cultivated throughout india, Parparticularly hot proviences Swarūpa (Botanical description): A large deciduous climber, branches slender pendulous bending downwards. Stem papery creamy white to grey in colour. Leaves 5-10 cm long ovate round, accuminate apex, glabrous, 7-9 nerved and reticulately veined. Flower are arranged in laxed raceme, Diocious, yellow in colour often larger than the leaves, Male flower in clusters, female in solitary. Fruit is Drupe, pea sized, sub globose, red color on maturity. Flowers can be seen in june while fruits occur in November. Seeds broadly ellipsoid. Prayojya aṅga (Part used): Mūla (Roots), Kanda (Stem). Chemical constituents: It contains three crystalline substances Giloin, Giloinin, and Gilosterol along with these it also contains Berberine. Preparation of Gudūcī satva: The fresh stem should be cut in small pieces, it properly soaked in a 4 parts of water over night. After soaking next day it is macerated well. Then the water with the contents kept undisturbed to allow the particles to settle down. The water portion removed carefully the sedimented satva is dried stored in the air tight containers

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Madhava Nidanam (Part 1) (Purvārdḍha, Chapter 2, verse 2):

मिथ्याहारविहारभ्यां दोषा ह्यामाशयाश्रया: । बहिर्निरस्य कोष्ठाग्नि ज्वरदा: स्यू रसानुगा: ।। २।।
answer_text: The Doṣas, provoked by indulgence in improper foods and behavior, enter the Āmāśaya (stomach) and drive out the digestive fire from there. They follow the Rasa dhātu (chyle) to spread throughout the body and give rise to fever. As this is important of all the diseases, Jvara (fever) is to be studied in the beginning (of the study of diseases). It is important because it afflicts the beings before any other disease, it is the strongest of all diseases, it troubles the body, organs and the mind, it invariably affects during birth and death; it invades all the living beings of static and mobile nature and the other diseases are not having such qualifications. As said in Caraka, ‘‘Jvara troubles body, organs and mind; it is like elder one to all other diseases and it is most powerful. The God himself had said that fever was very important disease. If afflicts the living beings during both the birth and death. (Ca. ci. 3). And there is no living being that is not burnt (affected) by fever (Ca. ci. 3). It is also said in Pālakāpya (Hastyāyurveda, Mahārogasthana, 9th chapter), ‘‘The fever afflicting Nāgas (elephants) is calleed ‘Pākala’; ‘Abhitāpa’ in horses; for cows, it is īśvara and in human beings it is Jvara. Pralāpa is the name given to fever that afflicts goats and sheep; Alasa in camels; Haridra in buffalloes; Mrgaroga in stags and deers, Abhighata in birds, Indramada in the fish, Pakṣapāta in the flies and the fever in snakes is called, 'Aksika'. In some other reference, Nīlikā is the name given to the fever afflicting the water, ‘Uṣara’ to that of earth and Koṭara is that one afflicting trees. 'Through ‘‘Dakṣāpamāna…………’’ etc., the initial origination of fever is being explained. Nihśvāsa (exhalation) is shown here as the outrage of lord, Siva. Suśruta says that it is formed out of the fire of anger of Rudra. (Su. u. t. 39). On the fore-head of angry Rudra, the third eye is created which is of fiery in nature. From the fire of anger, fiery arrow is created. As Caraka said, The lord has created the eye on the forehead and burnt the demons with that eye. He has created an arrow which was burnt in the fire of anger and which destroyed the ritual of Dakṣa, who insulted, him (Ca. ci. 3). This story of the origination of fever is detailed in Caraka Cikitsa, third chapter. By this, the distant reason for on set of fever is explained. Had it not been originated at the above juncture, the fever would never occur inspite of inducing the aetiological factors of that disease, says Bhattaraharicandra. This statement does not help much in the mangement of fever. Hence other commentators explain the story of incidence of fever in the following way–i.e. Anger denotes the Taijasa (fiery light) and anger itself is related to the fire element. Caraka also said ‘‘Pitta increases by anger”. (Ca. ci. 3) Hence it is established that in all fevers anti-Pitta management is to be adopted. Vāgbhaṭa said, there is no heat without. Pitta and there is no fever without heat. Therefore one should use anti-Pitta drugs and foods in fever and not the pitta provocative ones as they increase fever.'' (Vā. ci. 1). Because of this reason only, Caraka advocates bitter tasted drugs and foods as anti-Pitta material to facilitate digestion of undigested stuff (Ama) in just-afficted fever in thé place of pungent, sour and salty foods and drugs which increase pitta. In his words-''In just afflicted fever, skipping food, application of Sveda therapy and waiting to give foods and drugs, administration of porridge and bitter tasted drugs are adopted to facilitate the digestion of undigested Dosas''. (Ca. ci. 3). Some other commentators interpret in this way-''As fever is originated from the anger of lord Rudra, it is devine and the necessity of performing worship to this disease is indicated here.’’ As said by Videha–‘‘Jvara is pacified by worship’’. In Harivamsa, it is said, ''Jvara has three legs, three heads, six hands i and nine-eyes. It keeps shelling ashes, very fiery and equal to yama, the death-God. (probably this is indicative of the shape of the super micro-organism which may be discovered in future as the one responsible for causing and spreading fever). Though it is of many types, fever is said to be eight types precisely. These eight are ex- plained in the context of Samprāpti (pathogenesis).. The Doşas provoked by the indulgence of improper foods and behaviour, enter the Amāśaya and drive out the digestive fire from there, they follow the rasa dhātu, the chyle (to spread all over the body) and give rise to fever. Sweating, lightness of the body, itching sensation, ulceration in the mouth, sneezing and desire for food are the features of an individual who got relieved of fever. 75 (Su. u. 39)
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Purvārdḍha, Chapter 2, verse 2.

करोत्यादौर तथा पित्तं त्वक्स्थं दाहमतीव चे । तस्मिन् प्रशान्ते त्वितरी कुरुतः शीतमन्ततः द्वावेतौर में दाहशीतादिज्वरौ के संसर्गजौ के स्मृतौर । दाहपूर्वस्तयोः कष्टः कृच्छुसाध्यतमश्च सः ॥47॥
answer_text: (SS. Ut. 39. 59-61) When kapha is vitiated in the trunk after pitta has been vitiated and located in the extremities, fever manifests with the trunk being cold and the extremities warm. When the vitiated kapha and vata are lodged in the skin, they generate fever preceded by cold rigors where after the pitta turns the body warm. When the pitta lodged in the skin produces fever first, the other two dosas make the body cold. These two types of fevers dāhapūrva (the one preceded by heat) and śītapūrva (the one preceded by feeling of cold) are generated by the combination of two dosas. The dahapiirva type of fever is a troublesome disease and is very difficult to cure. 44-47
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Nidānasthāna, Chapter 2, verse 47.
context: करोत्यादौर तथा पित्तं त्वक्स्थं दाहमतीव चे । तस्मिन् प्रशान्ते त्वितरी कुरुतः शीतमन्ततः द्वावेतौर में दाहशीतादिज्वरौ के संसर्गजौ के स्मृतौर । दाहपूर्वस्तयोः कष्टः कृच्छुसाध्यतमश्च सः ॥47॥

answer_text: (SS. Ni. 1.34- 38) There could be vomiting and burning sensation, if prana vata gets avaraṇa (encompassed, surrounded) by pitta. There would be debil- ity, loss of strength, stupor and bad taste in the mouth, if prana vāta gets disturbed by kapha. Udāna vāta when encompassed by pitta generates burning sensation, fainting, giddiness and exhaustion; if it is encompassed by kapha, it generates loss of perspiration, loss of enthusiasm, poor digestive ability and feeling of cold. Samāna vāta encompassed by pitta, gives rise to perspiration, burning sensation, rise in temperature and fainting. If it is encom-passed by kapha, it generates blockage to elimination of urine mixed with blood and there is heaviness of the lower limbs and feeling of cold. Vyana vata encompassed by pitta gives rise to burning sensation, abnormal movements of the body parts and exhaustion; if encompassed by kapha, it leads to stiffness of the body like a log, pain, and swell- ing. 22-26

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Madhava Nidana (Laghutrayi) (Nidānasthāna, Chapter 22):

वातोपद्रवानाहविसर्पेत्यादि । वाता इति वातविकाराः कार्यकारणयोरभेदोप चारात् । वातादिति पाठे तु वाता ये पक्षवधादय इति योज्यम् । शूनमित्यादि शूनं सशोर्थम । सुप्तत्वचं स्पर्शानभिज्ञत्वगिन्द्रियम् ।।- अव्याहतगतिर्यस्य का स्थानस्थः का प्रकृतिस्थितः । वायुः स्यात् सोऽधिकं जीवेद्वीतरोगः समाः शतम् ॥८०॥ इति श्रीमाधवकरविरचिते माधवनिदाने वातव्याधिनिदानं समाप्तम् ॥ ॥ इदानीं पञ्चविधस्यापि प्रकृतिस्थस्य वायोर्लिङ्ग कार्यं चाहअव्याहतेत्यादि । यस्येति पुरुषस्य अव्याहतगतिरनवरुद्धमार्गः स्थानस्थः स्वाश्रयव्यवस्थितः प्रकृतिस्थितोऽक्षीणश्चा- प्रवृद्धः एतद्विशेषणत्रयं हेतु-हेतुमद्रावेन योज्यम् । वीतरोमो नीरोगः कफ-पित्तदुष्टरपि प्रेरकवातेनान्तरीयकत्वात् । अधिके समाः शतमिति पञ्च दिनाधिकें सविंशं वर्षशतम् । यदाह वराह आयुर्निरूपणेसमाः षधिर्देहैंच्ना मनुजकरिणां पञ्च निशाः । इत्यादि इति श्रीविजयरक्षितकृतायां मधुकोशव्याख्यायां वातव्याधिनिदानं प्रमाप्तम् से कार्यालय से ही कर मार्च अप्रैल - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
answer_text: The above passage starting from the term visarpa, etc. indicates features of the vātaja variety of complications. The cause and results are mutually related to each other so the term vāta has been used to denote the diseases related to vāta and not the vāta itself. Thus, it could also mean the stroke and other diseases. Apart from these, the commentary only repeats the original text. Normalcy of vāta If vāta having powers of unlimited movement remains in its normal locations, it helps man to live a hundred years without any disease. The passage starting from avyāhata refers to the characteristics of the natural winds of five types. The term Avyāhatagati signifies the uninterrupted pathway. Sthānastha means the one located in its original place. The term prakrtistha means one that is in harmony with the nature. The term vitaroga refers to the one away from any disease. It may be noted that even if kapha and pitta are not in equilibrium, vāta, the driving force, does not make room for any disease when it is in normalcy. Over hundred years means five days above one hundred and twenty years. About the age limit, one could recall the statement of Vārāhamihira who suggested that 60 into 2 and 5 that is 125 is the figure that denotes in terms of years the age of man and elephants. Thus concludes the Chapter on Vātavyādhi MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON VĀTA DISEASES INCLUDING PARALYSIS AND GAIT OF VARIOUS SORTS Paralysis signifies loss of purposeful or directed movement that oc¬ curs due to neurological disorders. It is the total loss of voluntary motor function produced from severe cortical or pyramidal tract damage. It can occur in cerebrovascular disorders, degenerative neu¬ romuscular disease, trauma, tumors or central nervous system infec¬ tion. Severe paralysis could be an early indicator of a life-threatening disorder, such as Guillain-Barre syndrome. Paralysis can be local or widespread, symmetrical or asymmetrical, transient or permanent and spastic or flaccid. It is normally classified according to location and severity as paraplegic (paralysis of the legs), quadriplegic (permanent paralysis of the arms, legs, and body lie low the level of the spinal lesion) or hemiplegic (unilateral paraly- sis of varying severity and permanence) or bilateral (diplegic). In- complete paralysis with profound weakness (paresis) may precede total paralysis in some patients. The symptoms of this disease have been noticed as emerging also due to following medical disorders: Amyotrophic, Bell’s palsy, Botu- lism, Brain abscess, Brain tumor, Cerebrovascular, Accident (CVA), Conversion disorder, Encepha-litis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, Head trauma, Migraine headache, Multiple sclerosis, Myasthenia gravis, Neurosyphilis, Parkinson’s disease, Peripheral nerve trauma, Periph- eral neuropathy, Poliomye-litis, Rabies, Seizure disorders, Spinal cord injury, Spinal cord tumors, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Syringo- myelia, Thoracic aortic aneurysm, Transient ischemic attack (TIA) and Western encephalitis. One can discuss some of the major types of vata disorders as per the following discriptions of various symptoms as identified by the modern medicine. MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON PARESTHESIA Paresthesia is an abnormal and unpleasant sensation or combination of sensations normally described as numbness, prickling, or tingling felt along peripheral nerve pathways. The disorder is generally de¬ scribed by the patients as numbness or as a prickly, stinging, or burn- ing feeling. Paresthesia can occur suddenly or gradually and might be transient or permanent. A common sign of many neurologic disorders, paresthesia can also result from certain systemic disorders or drug effects. It can reflect damage or irritation of the parietal lobe, thalamus, spinothalamic tract or spinal or peripheral nerves that are the neural circuit that transmits and interprets sensory stimuli. The sign of this disease could develop also due to following medical disorders: Arterial occlusion (acute), arteriosclerosis obliterans, ar- thritis, brain tumor, buerger’s disease, cerebrovascular accident (CVA), diabetes mellitus, guillain-barre syndrome, head trauma, heavy metal or solvent poisoning, herniated disk, herpes zoster, hy- perventilation syndrome, hypocalcemia, migraine headache, mul- tiple sclerosis (MS) and peripheral nerve trauma. Different types of gait Gait refers to the style of walking. Different types of gaits have been identified by the modern science and as such, they relate to neuro¬ logical problems or the vala disorders. In this connection, it may be noted that Ataxic gait is the symptom of unsteady, staggering gait pattern. A bizarre gait has no obvious organic basis; rather, it is gen¬ erated unconsciously by the person with a somatoform disorder (hys- terical neurosis) or consciously by a malingerer. The gait has no con- sistent pattern. It can mimic an organic impairment but has a more theatrical or bizarre quality with key elements missing or leg "pa- ralysis” with normal reflexes and motor strength. Its manifestations can include wild gyrations, exaggerated stepping, leg dragging, or mimicking such uncommon walks as that of a tightrope walker. Propulsive gait or Festinating gait This symptom relates to a walking pattern characterized by a rigid, stopped posture and the relative inability to oppose forward momen- tum. In this condition, the patient’s head and neck are bent forward; her flexed, stiffened arms are held away from the body; her fingers are extended; and her knees and hips are stiffly bent. During ambulation, this posture results in a forward shifting of the body’s center of gravity and consequent impairment of balance, causing in- creasingly rapid, short, shuffling steps with involuntary festination and lack of control over forward motion. Propulsive gait is a major sign of the Parkinson’s disease related again to the vāta disorders. It develops in a progressive degeneration of the ganglia that are prima¬ rily responsible for muscle movement. Because this develops gradu- ally and its effects are normally wrongly attributed, propulsive gait normally goes unreported until severe disability emerges. The symp- toms of this disease have been noticed as emerging also due to fol- lowing medical disorders: Carbon monoxide poisoning, Manganese poisoning and Parkinson’s disease. Scissors gait This is a gait marked by excessive hip adduction in swing phase. In this condition, the swing leg crosses in front of the stance leg. This vala induced symptom of the gait is seen in patients with an upper motor neuron lesion, and is accompanied by spasticity. Resulting from bilateral spastic paresis (diplegia), scissors gait affects both legs and has little or no effect on the arms. The patient’s legs flex slightly at the hips and knees, so she looks as if she were crouching. With each step, her thighs add act and her knees hit or cross in a scissors like movement. Her steps are short, reguiar, and laborious, as if she were wading through water. Her feet might be plantar flexed and turned inward, with a shortened Achilles tendon; consequently, she walks on her toes or on the balls of her feet and can scrape her toes on the ground. The sign of this disease could develop also due to following medical disorders: Cerebral palsy, cerebrovascular acci¬ dent, cervical spondylolysis with myelopathy, hepatic failure, mul- uple sclerosis, pernicious anemia, spinal cord trauma, spinal cord tumor, syphilitic meningomyelitis (inflammation of spinal cord) and syringomyelia (development of a cyst or cavities in the spinal cord). Spastic gait or Hemiplegic gait This type of gait refers to a stiff movement of the legs while walking, usually the result of an upper motor neuron lesion (that is again vāta- induced) and spasticity in the muscles of the lower extremities. Spastic gait is sometimes referred to as paretic or weak gait. That is a stiff, foot-dragging walk generated by unilateral leg muscle hypertonicity. This gait demonstrates focal damage to the cortico¬ spinal tract. The affected leg becomes rigid, with a marked decrease in flexion at the hip and knee and possibly plantar flexion and equinovarus deformity of the foot. Because the patient’s leg does not swing normally at the hip or knee, her foot tends to drag or shuffle, scraping her toes on the ground. To compensate, the pelvis of the affected side tilts upward in an attempt to lift the toes, causing the patient’s leg to abduct and circumduct. In addition, arm swing is hindered on the same side as the affected leg. Spastic gait normally develops after a period of flaccidity (hypoto- nicity) in the affected leg. Whatever the cause, the gait is normally permanent once it develops. The sign of this disease could develop also due to following medical disorders: Brain abscess, brain tumor, cerebrovascular accident, head trauma, and multiple sclerosis. Stoppage gait This is a gait in that the foot is lifted high to clear the toes. There is no heel strike, and the toes hit the ground first. The vata-induced symp- toms stoppage gait is produced from foot-drop generated by weak- ness or paralysis of pretibial and peroneal muscles, normally from lower motor neuron lesions. Foot-drop causes the foot to hang with the toes pointing down, causing the toes to scrape the ground during ambulation. To compensate, the hip rotates outward and the hip and knee flex, in an exaggerated fashion to lift the advancing leg off the ground. The foot is thrown forward and the toes hit the ground first, producing an audible slap. The rhythm of the gait is normally regular, with even steps and normal upper body posture and arm swing. Stop- page gait can be unilateral or bilateral and permanent or transient, depending on the site and type of neural damage. The sign of this disease could develop also due to following medical disorders: Guillain-barre syndrome, herniated lumber disk, multiple sclerosts, peroneal muscle atrophy, peroneal nerve trauma, poliomyclitis, poly- neuropathy and spinal cord trauma. Waddling gait This is a sort of gait in that the feet are wide apart making the patient walk like a duck (vartaka). It appears as if he/she is walking under water. This morbidity is also related to the vāta disorders. It occurs in coxa vora and double congenital hip displacement when lordosis is present. Waddling gait is a significant symptom of muscular dystro¬ phy, spinal muscle atrophy or, rarely, congenital nip displacement. It might be present when the child begins to walk or can appear some- time later. The gait is produced from deterioration of the pelvic girdle muscles, the glutens medius, hip flexors and hip extensors. Weakness in these muscles hinders stabilization of the weight-bearing hip dur- ing walking, causing the opposite hip to drop, and the trunk to lean in an attempt to maintain balance. Typically, the legs assume a wide stance and the trunk is thrown back to further improve stability, exaggerating lordosis and abdominal protrusion. In severe cases, leg and foot muscle contractures generate equinovarus deformity of the foot combined with circumduction or bowing of the legs. The sign of this disease could develop also due to congenital hip dysplasia and muscular dystrophy. e the comment of the com and the control of the c e the content of the con and the control of the control and the control of the ll and in the content of the co

Complications of chardi 1999 at The implications of vomiting include cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, thirst, mental torpidity, heartache, and feeling of being in darkness. Thus concludes the Chapter on Chardi. MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON VOMITING Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth. Characteristically preceded by nausea, vomiting is produced from a coordinated sequence of abdominal muscle contractions and reverses esophageal peristalsis. A common symptom of Gastro-intestinal disorders, vomiting also occurs with fluid and electrolyte imbalances, infections, and meta¬ bolic, endocrine, labyrinthine, central nervous system (CNS) and cardiac disorders. It can also result from drug therapy, surgery, and radiation. Vomiting occurs normally during the first trimester of pregnancy, but its subsequent development can indicate complications. It can also result from stress, anxiety, pain, alcohol intoxication, overeating, or ingestion of distasteful foods or liquids. The physicians should scrutinize the abdomen for distension and auscultate for bowel sounds and bruits. One should palpate for rigid¬ ity and tenderness and test for rebound tenderness. Next, palpate and percuss the liver for enlargement. Examine other body systems if they are inappropriate. It may be noted that projectile vomiting unaccompanied by nausea can demonstrate increased intracranial pressure, a life-threatening emergency. If this occurs in a patient with CNS injury, the physician should quickly check his vital symptoms. Be alert for widened pulse pressure or bradycardia. AŚVAGANDHĀ Latin: Withania somnifera Dunal. Fam: Solanaceae Hin: Asgandha, Asgandh Eng: Winter cherry Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): The equivalent words of Aśvagandha are all the titles of ‘Aśva’ (Horse) as a perfix and ‘Gandha’ aroma as suffix including these it also has Varāha karṇī, Varadā, Baladā and Kuṣṭha Gandhinī. Guṇa karma (Properties and indications): Aśvagandha is Tikta (Bitter) and Kaṣāya (Astringent) in taste, Uşnavīrya (Hot in potency), subsides Vāta and Kapha doşa, Atiśukrala (Increases semen), Balya (Strength promoters), Rasayana (Rejuvenator). It cures Switra (Vitiligo), Sotha (Inflammation) and Kṣaya (Emaciation). Utpattisthāna (Natural territory): It is found in temprate and drier parts of Western regions. Nagaur district of Madya Pradesh is the main source of market drug. Swarūpa (Botanical description): An erect under shrub reaches 3-4 ft. in height Stem cylindrical, branched, covered with stellate tomentum. Leaves 8 cm. long, and 5 cm. broad, ovate-oblong, entire margins, acute apex, tapering to the base and covered with glandular hair. Flowers greenish-yellow about 5 together in subsessile umbelliform cymes. Fruits berry, globose, 1.5 cm. in diameter, yellow or red when ripe. Prayojya anga (Part used): Mūla (Roots). Bheda (Varieties): There are two types of Ashwagandha. a. Ashwagandha b. Nāgorī. Ashwagandha. The roots look different. Nāgorī ashwagandha is identified as Withania ashwagandha. 32 JA-413 Chemical constituents: Alkaloids- Somnifera, Essential oils, Crystalline compounds Withanolide and Hentriacontane

Note: It has become a controversial drug. According to Bhāvamisra its appearance and fragrance are like Kankola and Kusta. According to few scholars the source plant Prunus cerasns Linn. (Rosaceae) is taken as Elavalukam. Prunus cerasns Linn. (Rosaceae): It is a tree, reaches upto a 4-10 m. Leaves 5-10 cm long and 2-3 cm wide, broadly ovate, acuminate and serrated. question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Dugdha Varga, Chapter 13, verse 1006):

धारोष्ण गोपयो बल्य लघु शीत सुधासमम् । दीपनञ्च त्रिदोषघन तद्वाराशिशिरं त्यजेत् ।।२४।। धारोष्ण शस्यते गव्यं धाराशीतन्तु माहीषम् । श्रृतोष्णमाविक पथ्यं श्रृतशीतमजापयः ।।२५ आम क्षीरमभिष्यन्दि गुरु श्लेष्मामवर्वनम् । ज्ञेयं सर्वमपथ्यं तु गव्यमाहिषवर्जितम् ।।२६।। नारीक्षीर त्वाममेव हित न तु शृतं हितम् । शृतोष्ण कफवातघ्न शृतशीतन्तु पित्तनुत् ।।१७।। अन्द्वोदकं क्षीरशिष्टमामाल्लघुतरं पयः । जलेन रहित दुग्धमतिपक्क यथा यथा । तथा तथा गुरु स्निग्धं वृष्य बलविवर्धनम् ।।२८।। क्षीरं तत्कालसूताया घनं पीयूषमुच्यते । नष्टदुग्धस्य पक्रस्य पिण्डः प्रेन्तः किलाटकः ।। २९।। अपक्कमेव यन्नष्ट क्षीरशाकं हि तत्पयः 11 ३ 011 दध्ना तक्रेण वा नष्ट दुग्धं बद्धं सवाससा । द्रवभावेन सहितं तक्रपिण्डः स उच्यते । । ३ १ । ! नष्टदुग्धभव नीरं मोरट जैज्जटोऽब्रवीत् । पीयूषञ्च किलाटञ्च क्षीरशाक तथैव च ।।३२।। तक्रपिण्डं इमे वृष्या बृहणा बलवर्डनाः । गुरवः श्लेष्मला हृद्या वातपत्तिविनाशनः । । ३ ३ । । दीप्ताग्नीनां विनिद्राणां विद्रधौ चाभिपूजिताः । मुखशोषतृषादाहरक्तपित्तज्वरप्रणुत् ।। लघुर्बलकरो रुच्यो मोरटः स्यात्सितायुतः ।।३४।।
answer_text: Dhārosṇādi dugdha (Fesh cows milk) is Balya (Promotes strength), Laghu (Light for digestion), Śīta vīrya (Cold in potency), similar to nectar, Dīpana (Appetizer), aggravates all Tridosas, But if it is kept for long time, it becomes cold should be avoided. It is to be comsume by boiling properly. Dhārosṇādi is consumed in hot state in case of cows milk is ideal. Dhārośita, is consumed in cold state in case Buffalo’s milk. Boiled hot milk is ideal in case of sheeps milk, boiled and cooled is ideal in case of Goat’s milk. Uncooked milk of animals other than cow and buffalo acts as Abhiṣyanḍī (Block the channels), Guru (Heavy for digestion), increases Kapha and Ama (Undigested food) and it should be considered as unfit. Stree dugdha is ideal in uncooked state, it should not be boiled. Naturally boiled milk aggravates Kapha and subsides Vāta, boiled and cooled milk increases pitta, if half part of water is added, then bolied reduces it to till milk part remains, it is more Laghu (Light for digestion) compare than unboiled milk. It becomes excessive boiled without adding any water it is Guru (Heavy for digestion), Snigdha (Oilyness), Vrsya (Aphrodisiac) and Balya (Promotes strength). Pīyūṣa, Kilāṭa, Kṣīraśaka andTakrapiṇḍa: Milk of the cow, buffalos etc. are taken soon after the delivery is called as Pīyūsa. Spoiled milk is boiled till it becomes solidified is called Kilāṭaka Milk which becomes sour without boiling is know as Kṣīraśāka Milk is make sour by adding sour substances like dadi, takra etc., it is tied in a thick cloth to remove much of it’s water, the remaining solid portion is called as Takrapinda. As per jejjaṭa is called as Moraṭa. Pīyūṣa, Kilāṭa, Kṣīraśaka and Takrapinḍa all these are Vṛṣya (Aphrodisiac), Bṛhmaṇa (Stoutning), Balya (Promotes strength), Guru (Heavy for digestion), Increases Kapha doşa, Hrdya (Useful in cardiac diseases), subsides Vāta and Pitta, Dīpana (Appetizer), Vinidranam (Insomnia), suffering from Vidradi (Abcess). If Mōrata is associated with sugar, it is Laghu (Light for digestion), Balya (Promotes strength) and Rūcya (Promotes taste). It cures Mukhaśoṣa (Dryness in mouth), Tṛṣṇā (Thrist), Dāha (Burning sensation), Raktapitta (Haemorrages) and Jwara (Fever)
citation: Bhavaprakasha Nighantu — Dugdha Varga, Chapter 13, verse 1006
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Dugdha Varga, Chapter 13, verse 1006.

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Haritakyadi Varga, Chapter 1, verse 177):

शाकम्भरीयं कथितं गडाख्यं रोमकं तथा ।। २४ २ ।। गडाख्यं लघु वातघ्नमत्युष्णं भेदिपित्तलम् । तीक्ष्णोष्णं चापि सुक्ष्मझाभिष्यन्दिकटुपाकि च ।।२४३।। सामुद्रं यत्तु लवणमक्षीवं वशिरञ्ठ तत् । समुद्रजं सागरजं लवणोदधिसम्भवम् ।।२४४।। सामुद्रं मधुरं पाके सतिक्तं मधुरं गुरु । नात्युष्णं दीपनं भेदि सक्षारमविदाहि च । श्लेष्मलं वातनुत्तीक्ष्णं मरूक्षं नातिशीतलम् ।।२४५.।।
answer_text: Digestive diseases: In conditions like severe Āṭisarā (Diarrhoea) Pravāhikā (Dysentery), due to the excess fluid loss, it is so necessary to used saline solution intravenously. Vamaka (Emetic) and Virecaka (Purgative): It acts as both Vamaka (Emetic) and Virecaka (Purgative) in excess and still excess dose respectively. Krimi roga (Work infestation): Administered by the rectum destroys and brings away Krmi (Worm) from the larger bowels. Respiratory disease: The common salt or rock salt is used as good Kaphahara (Expectorant), in case of pneumonia, it is applied externally in the form of seka. it looses the accumulated mucus and expels it. In conditions like Pinasa (Running nose), Śiraśūla (Headache), etc the nasya is given with saline solutionis benficial. It is used as a gargle in Galaroga (Chronic thoat diseases or ulceration). Poisoning: It is valuable antitode in case of Silver nitrate poisoning. External uses: The saline solution is used for cleaning the Vrna (Wounds). it prevents the growth of infections. answer_text: Performing hard and arduous tasks results in the disease traumatic chest (urahkṣata) which is the etiology for consumption as well and hence, this disease is being discussed along with etiology in the context. Destruction of digestive fire causes diarrhoea. By applying, the term api in the text Vidbhedoagnivadhadapi it is underlined that diarrhoea may occur even without disturbance of digestive fire due to the influence of the consumption.) The person afflicted by traumatic chest is emaciated not only due to trauma alone, but he also suffers from the depletion of semen and essential fluid of the body, the ojas, that could be caused by over-indulgence in sexual activities. S. 11.13) The cases of urahkṣata or traumatic chest, pain in the chest, vomiting of blood, cough are prominent if trauma is present, while urine mixed with blood, pain in the flanks, back and waist (hips) are predominant if only emaciation is present. 30 The passage starting from urorugityādi refers to the peculiar characteristics of the disease. Specific cough means that phlegm of putrefied nature, black or yellow in colour and mixed with blood is expectorated. The patient passes urine that is red in colour and there could be even blood mixed with urine. Prognosis of kṣatakṣīna-emaciation due to traumatic chest (CS. Ci. S. 11.14). t> <<= The condition is curable when the clinical manifestations are mild, appetite is good, general condition of the patient is satisfactory and the disease is of recent origin. Nevertheless, if the disease has remained over one year, it might persist throughout life. If all the Clinical features described above are present in the patient the disease would prove incurable. 31 The passage starting from the term alpa explains the curability of the disease kṣatakṣīna. The term alpa stresses that the impact of disease is minimal. Thus concludes the Chapter on Rājayakṣmā. MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON KŞAYA OR TUBERCULOSIS Tuberculosis is an infectious disease generated by the causative or¬ ganism intracellular parasite M tuberculosis. The disease primarily affects lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis. It can also affect intestine, meninges, bones and joints, lymph glands, skin and other tissues of the body. The disease is normally chronic with varying clinical manifestations. The disease also affects animals like cattle and such cases are known as bovine tuberculosis, which can some- times be transmitted to man. Pulmonary tuberculosis, the most sig¬ nificant form of tuberculosis, which affects man, is normally dis¬ cussed under the heading of tuberculosis. TB, as the disease is called in short, most commonly affects the lungs but also can involve almost any organ of the body. Its infection usu¬ ally occurs initially in the lobe of the lungs. The body’s immune sys- tem, however, can stop the bacteria from continuing to reproduce. Thus, the immune system can make the lung infection inactive. On the other hand, if the body’s immune system cannot contain the TB bacteria, the bacteria could become active in the lungs and spread elsewhere in the body. In the yore, this disease was referred to as "consumption" be¬ cause without treatment, these patients often would waste away. A person can become infected with tuberculosis bacteria when one inhales minute particles of infected sputum from the air. The bacteria, get into the air when someone who has a tuberculosis lung infection coughs, sneezes, shouts, or spits. People who are nearby can then possibly breathe the bacteria into their lungs. However, one does get TB by just touching the clothes or hands of someone infected. The disease is transmitted primarily from person to person by breathing infected air during close contact. M. tuberculosis is a facultative intracellular parasite, i.e., it is readily ingested by phagocytes and is resistant to intracellular killing. Of significance to man are the human and bovine strains. The human strain is accountable for the vast majority of cases. The bovine strain influences chiefly cattle and other animals. Regarding virulence, the Indian tubercle bacillus is said to be less virulent than the European bacillus. In recent years, a number of atypical mycobacieria have been isolated from man. These have been categorised into four groups: (i) photochromogens (for example M kansasii) (ii) scoto- chromogens (e.g., M. scrofulaceum), (iii) non-photochromogens (e.g., M miercellulsre or Battey bacillus); and, (iv) rapid growers (for example, M fortuitum). All these are chiefly saprophytic diseases akin to pulmonary tuberculosis and chronic cervical lymphadenitis. Non-specific infections have been reported to be widely prevalent in the southern part of India. The usual symptoms that occur with an active TB infection are a generalized tiredness or weakness, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. If the infection in the lung worsens, then further symptoms can include coughing, chest pain, coughing up of sputum and/or blood, and shortness of breath. If the infection spreads beyond the lungs, the symptoms will depend upon the organs involved. In the past, there was a form of atypical tuberculosis that was transmitted by taking unpasteurized milk. Related bacteria, called Mycobacterium bovis, caused this form of TB. This type of bacteria was a major cause of TB in children. Anyone can get TB, but certain people are at higher risk, including the people who live with individuals who have an active TB infection, the poor or homeless people, foreign-born people from countries that have an endemic prevalence of TB, nursing-home residents and prison inmates, the alcoholics and intravenous drug users, the people with diabetes, certain cancers, and HIV infection (the AIDS virus), and health-care workers. The disease continues a worldwide public health disorder despite the fact that the factor was discovered more than 100 years ago and highly effective drugs and vaccine are available making tuberculosis a preventable and curable disease. According to conservative estimates, there are 15-20 million cases of infectious tuberculosis in the world. This infectious pool is maintained by the occurrence of 4-5 million new cases and the mortality of some 3 million patients each year. Dr Park has reminded that technologically advanced countries have achieved spectacular accomplishment in the control of tuberculosis. For example, from 1900 to 1980 tuberculosis death rate declined from 199 to 0.5 per 100, 000 in the United States. This decline started long before the advent of BCG or chemotherapy. Actually, the de- cline has been attributed to changes in the nonspecific determinants of the disease such as improvement in the standard of living and the standard of life of the people coupled with the proper application of available technical knowledge and health resources. The disorder of tuberculosis is severe in the developing countries that account for more than three fourths of the cases in the world and where the majority of cases are never diagnosed at all; still less are correctly treated. Tuberculosis continues to be a major public health disorder in India. Since the national reporting system is defective, the only reliable source of information on the magnitude of the tuberculosis disorder has been the population sample surveys. Many such surveys have been conducted in the country during the past two decades or so. The disease is more prevalent in males than in females. Tuberculosis affects all ages. Developing countries show a sharp rise in infection rates from infancy to adolescence. In India such infection is aver¬ agely 1 per cent in the below 5 age group. The infection index climbs to about 30 per cent at age 15 years. In the developed countries, the disease is more common in the elderly only, Tuber-culosis is not a hereditary disease. However, there have been studies that demon¬ strate that inherited susceptibility is a significant risk determinant. Man has no inherited immunity against tuberculosis. It is obtained consequently of natural infection or BCG vaccination. Past infection with atypical mycobacteria is also credited with certain amount of naturally obtained immunity. It is now known that both delayed hypersensitivity and obtained resistance to tuberculosis are cell- mediated responses. In most cases, the cellular immunity proves adequate to limit further multiplication and spread of bacilli

answer_text: Home Kh The passage starting from iti refers to the characteristics of the curable and incurable varieties of the disease. The ailment is cured in condition of the availability of the best foursome of treatment which implies an efficient physician, effective drugs, a good nurse and a fit patient. The Kāsa of old age can be prolonged while the kāsa caused due to irregular diet and regimen can be cured in a relatively shorter time. Thus concludes the Chapter on Kāsa. MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON COUGH Cough has been identified as a forceful and violent expiratory effort that is preceded by a preliminary inspiration. Productive coughing is the body’s mechanism for clearing airway passages of accumulated secretions that normal mucociliary action does not remove. It is a sudden, forceful, noisy expulsion from the lungs of air that contains sputum or blood or both. The sputum’s colour, consistency, and odour provide significant clues about the patient’s condition. It can occur as a single cough or as paroxysmal coughing and it can be voluntarily induced, although it is normally a reflexive response to stimulation of the airway mucosa. Productive cough is the most regu- lar symptom in the category of various sorts of coughing. Simply defined, a productive cough is the one that involves mucus or exude that is expectorated. Normally due to a cardiovascular or respiratory disorder, productive coughing is produced from a severe or chronic infection that causes inflammation, oedema, and increased mucus production in the air- ways. However, this symptom can also result from acquired immu¬ nodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Inhalation of antigenic or irritating substances or foreign bodies also can produce a productive cough. Actually, the most common factor of chronic productive coughing is cigarette smoking, which generates mucoid sputum in colour rang¬ ing from clear to yellow to brown. Many patients minimize or overlook a chronic productive cough or accept it as normal. Such patients cannot seek medical attention until a related disorder that is such as dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest pain, weight loss or recurrent respiratory infections develop. The delay can lead to serious consequences because productive coughing is related with several life-threatening disorders and can harbinger airway oc¬ clusion from excessive secretions. A patient with a productive cough can develop severe respiratory dis¬ tress from thick or excessive secretions, broncho spasm, or fatigue: Therefore, the physician should examine him before taking his his¬ tory. The physician should note down vital symptoms and check the rate, depth, and rhythm of respirations. He should keep the patient’s airway patent and be prepared to provide supplemental oxygen if he becomes restless or confused or if his respirations become shallow, irregular, rapid or slow. He should remain alert for strider, wheezing, choking, or gurgling. The physician should remain alert for nasal flaring and cyanosis as well. A productive cough can indicate a severe life-threatening disorder. For example, coughing due to pulmonary oedema generates thin, frothy, pink sputum and coughing due to an asthmatic attack gener¬ ates thick, mucoid sputum. Blood-tinged or rust-coloured sputum might be generated from trauma due to coughing or from an underlying condition, such as a pulmonary infection or a tumor. Foul-smelling sputum might be gen- erated from an anaerobic infection, such as bronchitis or lung ab¬ scess. Similarly, a hacking cough is produced from laryngeal in¬ volvement, while a “brassy” tough one demonstrates major airway involvement. The physician should examine the patient's mouth and nose for congestion, drainage, or inflammation. It may be noted that a breath odour or Halitosis can be a symptom of pulmonary infec- tion. In some studies, it has been found that gastroesophageal reflux dis- ease (GERD) accounted for about 41% of cases of chronic cough in nonsmoking patients. If refluxed stomach acid is aspirated, it can produce coughing. Besides the productive type of cough, the scientists have also identi¬ fied a non-productive cough. This sort of cough is signified through a noisy, forceful expulsion of air from the lung that does not involve sputum or blood expulsion. Moreover, there is a barking cough signi- fied by oedema of the larynx and surrounding tissues. This sort of cough is more prevalent among children as their airways are smaller in diameter. Because her airway is narrow, a child with a productive cough can quickly develop airway occlusion and respiratory distress from thick or excessive secretions. Causes of productive cough in children include asthma, bronchiectasis, bronchitis, severe bronchi¬ olitis, cystic fibrosis and pertussis. Several studies indicate a significant link between GERD and asthma. The findings of these studies show that up to 60% of people with asthma have gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also, whereas such case occurs enly with 10% of the general population. GERD can affect asthma when refluxed acid from the stomach is aspirated into the airways and lungs and can make breathing difficult and generate wheeze and cough The sign of this coughing could develop also due to following medi- cal disorders: Actinomyocosis, aspiration pneumonitis, pasthma (acute), branchiectasis, bronchitis (chronic), chemical pneumonitis, common cold, legionnaire’s disease, lung abscess (ruptured), lung cancer, no¬ cardiosis, north american blastomycosis, pneumonia, psittacosis, pulmonary, coccidioidomycosis, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary emphysema, tuberculosis, silicosis and tra¬ cheobronchitis. Modern science has identified the following types of cough: aneurys¬ mal, brassy, bronchial, chronic (that occurs daily for at least three weeks), diphtherial, dry (that is unaccompanied by sputum produc¬ tion). hacking, harsh. mois: (accompanied by loose mucus and exu¬ dates), paroxysmal, pulmonary, reflexive, trigeminal and whooping types of coughs. Moreover, an ear cough has also been identified. This is a reflex cough induced by irritation in the ear that stimulates Arnold's nerve

Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Guducyadi Varga, Chapter 3, verse 470):

ब्राह्मी कपोतवड्डा च सोमवल्ली सरस्वती । मण्डूकपर्णी माण्डूकी त्वाष्ट्री दिव्या महौषधी ।। २७९।। ब्राह्मी हिमासरा तिक्ता लघुर्मेध्या च शीतला । कषाया मधुरा स्वादुपाकाऽऽयुष्या रसायनी ।।२८.०।। स्वर्या स्मृतिप्रदा कुष्ठपाण्डुमेहास्त्रकासजित् । विषशोथज्वरहरी तद्वन्मण्डूकपर्णिनी ।। २८ १ ।।
answer_text: Digestive disease: The prepared paste of Bhūmyāmalakī with Takra cures Kāmalā (Jaundice) effectively. In case of Pravāhikā (Dysentry) the young tender parts of Bhūmyāmalakī administered in the form of Infusion. The bark as well as Gum used to treat condition like Atisāra (Diarrhoea), Prarāhikā (Dysentry). Menstural diseases: Bhūmyāmalikī roots taken with Rice water cures Pradara (Meno-mettroghia). The prepared decoction is used to treat Pradara (Meno-mettroghia) and Svetapradar (Leucorrhoea) Galactogogue action: Fresh roots added with milk is useful. External uses: The leaf paste is applied external over Vispoţa (Blisters), Vrṇa (Wounds) etc Skin aliments. Mātrā (Dosage): Swarasa: 10-20ml., Cūrṇa 3-6gms. BRĀHMI AND MANDŪKAPARNĪ Latin: Bacopa monnieri Linn, Fam: Scrophulariaceae Hin: Jalnim Eng: Thyme leaved gratila Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): Kapotavańkā, Somavallī and Sarswatī and those of Manḍūkaparṇī are Māṇḍūkī, Tvaṣṭrī, Divyā and Mahaausadhi. Guṇa karma (Properties and indications): Brāhmi is Sitā vīrya (Hot in potency), Sarā (Laxative), Tikta (Bitter) in taste, Laghu (Light for digestion), Mēdhya (Brain tonic), Sitala (Cold in action), Kaṣāya (Astringent), Madhura (Sweet) in taste, Madhura vipaka (Sweet in post digestive), Ayuṣyā (Increases life span), Rāsayana (Reguvenator), Swaryā Promotes good voice) and Smṛtipradā (Promotes intellect). It cures Kuṣṭa (Leprosy), Pāṇḍu (Anemia), Prameha (Diabeties), Raktavikara (Bleeding disorders), Kāsa (Cough), Visa (Posionous manifestations), Sotha (Inflammation) and Jwara (Fever).The properties and indications of Mandūkaparni is similar to that of Brāhmi. Note: Brāhmi and Mandūkaparni has become a contraversial drug. The various classics and Nighantus has given so many synonyms made the identity of Brāhmi and Mandūkparṇī so confusing. Earlier it was confused for Bacopa monnieri Wettst., as both were sold in the market by the name ‘Brahmi’. Nowadays the controversy has been resolved and it was confirmed that Brahmi is Bacopa monnieri Wettst. and Maṇḍūkaparṇī is Centella asiatica. Linn. As per P.V. Sharmaji both are synonymes of each other for the commenest source plant Manḍūkaparni (Centella acitica. Linn.) and considers B.monnieri Wettst. as Aindri. Utpattisthāna (Natural territory): It is found throughout India in wet and damp places. Swarūpa (Botanical description): It is a perennial creeping herb, grows upto 10-30cm.long. Leaves are oblanceolate, sessile, decussate, 4-18mm.long, and relatively thick. Flowers 8-10 mm., axillary, solitary, long linear, small pale blue-white in colour. Fruit capsule 5mm.long, narrowly ovoid, acute, pointed with style base, glaborous. Seeds 0.85mm., yellow-brown, ellipsoid and longitudinally channeled. Prayojya aṅga (Part used): Pañcāṅga (Whole plant). Chemical constituents: Alkaloid- Bramhine

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Guducyadi Varga, Chapter 3, verse 317):

answer_text: Latin: Calatropis Procera Linn. R. Br. Fam: Asclepiadaceae. Hin: Aak, Madar. Eng: Madar, Crown flower. Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): Guṇarūpa, Mandāra, Vasuka, Śvēta puṣpa, Sadā puşpa, Alarka and Pratāpa and that of Raktarka are Arkanama, Arkaparna, Vikīraṇa, Raktapuspa, Suklaphala and Asphota. Guna karma (Properties and indications): Both varties of Arka are Rechaka (Laxitive), cures diseases of Vāta, Kuṣṭa (Leprosy), Kaṇḍu (Itching), Viṣa (Posions manifestation), Vrṇa (Wounds), Plīhā roga (Splenic disorders), Gulma (Abdominal tumors), Arśas (Hemorrhoids), Diseases of Kapha, Udararoga (Abdominal disorders) and Sakrut kṛmi (Useful in intestinal worms). Flowers of both varieties are Vrsya (Aphrodisiac), Laghu (Light for digestion), Dīpana (Appetizers) and Pacaka (Digestive). It cures Aruchi (Aneroxia), Praseka (Excessive salivation), Arśa (Piles), Kāsa (Cough) and Swāsa (Dysponea). Flowers of red variety are Madhura (Sweet) and Tikta (Bitter) in taste, Sangrahī (Absorbents), cures Gulma (Abdominal tumors), Sotha (Inflammation), Kuṣta (Leprosy), Krmi (Worm infestations), Diseases of Kaphaja, Arśas (Piles), Viṣa ( Posions manifestation) and Rakta pitta (Haemorrages). Fruits of both varieties are Tikta (Bitter) and Lavaṇa (Salty) in taste, Uṣnavīrya (Hot in potency), Snigdha (Oilyness) and Laghu (Light for digestion). It cures Kusta (Leprosy), Gulma (Abdominal tumors) and Udararoga (Abdominal disorders) and it acts as Best Recaka (Purgative). Utpattisthāna (Natural territory): A weed which grown in drier areas throughout india. Bheda (Varieties): Bhāvamiśra has mentioned two varieties of Arka based on flowers colours viz. Suklarka (C. gigantea (Linn.) R.Br.) having white flowers, Raktarka (C.Procera (Ait.) R. Br. having red flowers. Their is not much difference in the Properties and indications of these varieties. Swarūpa (Botanical description): A spreading shrub or a small tree reaches upto 6-8 ft. Bark ash coloured and wrinkled. Leaves 5- 15 cm. long and 3-8cm. broad, opposite, grey-green, elliptic or obovate-oblong, accuminate- acute apex, Cordate base and sessile. Flowers waxy white, corolla pink arranged in umbellate cymes. Fruit, follicles, 7.5cm. long and 3.2 cm. broad, containing numerous seeds 1.5cm., black in colour. Prayojya añga (Part used): Mũla twak (Root bark). Chemical constituents: B.amyrin, Glycosides -Gigantoel and Isogigantoal and Isomeric Crystalline alcohols ŚVETA ARKA Latin: Calatropis gigantea R.Br. Fam: Asclepiadaceae. Hin: Aak, Madar. ng: Madar, Crown flower. Swarūpa (Botanical description): An erect shrub usually grows 8-10 ft high. Young part clothed with tomentum. Leaves, 10-20cm long and 6-10cm broad, opposite, elliptic or obovate-oblong, accuminate- acute apex, cordate base and sessile. Flowers, 3.7-5cm in diameter, purple red to white, 5 sepals and 5 petals, arranged in Umbellate cymes. Fruits, Follicles 10cm long containing numerous seeds with tufts of long silky hairs at one end. Prayojya anga (Part used): Mūla twak (Root bark). Chemical constituents: Caltoropins, Calotoxin, gigantin, giganteold etc

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Visa-Upavisa Varga, Chapter 7, verse 754):

अझनं यामुनं चापि कापोताझनमित्यपि । तत्तु स्रोतोऽझनं कृष्णं सौवीरं श्वेतमीरितम् ।।१३५।। वल्मीकशिखराकारं भिन्नमञ्नसन्निभम् । घृष्ट तु गैरिकाकारमेतत्वोतोञ्ननं स्मृतम् ।।१३५।। स्रोतोझनसमं जेयं सौवीरं तत्तु पाणडुरम् । स्रोतोऽझनं स्मृतं स्वादु चक्षष्यं कफपित्तनुत् ।।१३७।। कषायं लेखनं स्निग्थं ग्राहि च्छर्दिविषापहम् । सिध्मक्षयास्रहच्छीतं सेवनीयं सदा बुधेः ।।१३८।। स्रोतोऽझनगुणाः सर्वे सौवीरेऽपि मता बुधैः । किन्तु द्वयोरझनयोः श्रेष्ठ स्रोतोझन स्मृतम् ।।१३९।।
answer_text: Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): Yāmunam and Kāpotāñjanam. ĀVAPRAKĀŚA NIGHAN It is appear like peak of ant hill, black when breaking and red when rubbing on a stone lt is pale in appearance and properties are quite similar to añjana. Sauvira Guṇa karma (Properties and indications): Srōṭōñjana is Swadu (Palatable), Cakṣuṣyā (Good for eyes), subsides Kapha and Pitta, Kaṣāya (Astringent) in taste, Lekhana (Scarping), Snigdha (Oilyness), Grāhī (Absorbent) and Śīta vīrya (Cold in potency). It cures Chardi (Vomiting), Viṣa (Posionous manifestations), Sidma (Skin diseases), Kṣaya (Emaciation), and Diseases of Rakta. The wise person’s should always consume it regularly. The properties of Sauvīra is quite similar to the Añjana, but amongest both Añjana is superior
citation: Bhavaprakasha Nighantu — Visa-Upavisa Varga, Chapter 7, verse 754
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Visa-Upavisa Varga, Chapter 7, verse 754.

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Madhava Nidana (Laghutrayi) (Nidānasthāna, Chapter 3):

सन्निपातिकमाह वराहेत्यादि । वराहस्नेहः शूकरस्य मेदो मज्जा वा मांसाम्बु मांसप्रक्षालनोदकं तैः सदृशम् । सर्वरूपिणमिति उक्तवाताद्वतीसारत्रेयलक्षणयुक्तम् । एवंविध- मतीसारं दोपत्रयोद्रवं विद्यात् तं च कृच्छूसाध्यं त्रिदोपजत्वादेव ।।॥ तैस्तैभावैः शोचतोऽल्पाशनस्य वाष्पोष्मा वै वह्निमाविश्य जन्तोः । कोष्ठं गत्वा क्षोभयेत्तस्य रक्तं तच्चाधस्तात् काकणन्तीप्रकाशम् ॥॥ निर्गच्छेद्वै विड्विमिश्रं ह्यविड्वा निर्गन्धं वा गन्धवद्वाऽतिसारः । शोकोत्पन्नो दुश्चिकित्स्योऽतिमात्रं रोगो वैद्यैः केष्ट एष प्रदिष्टः ॥१ ॥ - - - -
answer_text: The above passage starting from the term vardha, etc. indicates features of the diarrhoea caused by sannipata. The main symptom of the disease is the smell of raw or uncooked flesh. The term sneha underlines the fat. The tridosaja or sannipata variety of diarrhoea should be considered as the one curable only with difficulty. e - Diarrhoea due to grief (SS. Ut. 40.13.2-15.1) In persons who are deeply afflicted with grief (due to loss of wealth, kith and kin and the like) and who take little or no eatables, the heat generated through tears, gets to the digestive fire and reaches the alimentary canal and ultimately disturbs the blood. The blood resembling the seed of kakanantī gets expelled out of the body either mixed with faeces or alone and with or without bad smell. असाध्यलक्षणमाह मांसेत्यादि । कृथितमिव पूतितां यतमिव । कर्दमम् आविल- मिवाम्भः कर्दमाम्भः अथवा कर्दमनिधम-भोनिर्म च । तथा मेदःप्याख़कल्पमिति कल्पशब्दो मेदःप्रभूतिभिस्त्रिभिः सम्बध्यते इति गयदासः । यकृदिव यकृत्खण्डमिव । पक्वजम्बूफलाभं स्निग्धकृष्णम् । कृष्णम् अख़नाभम् । नीलं चाषपक्षप्रतिमम् । नन् पैतिके कृष्णत्वं पठितं न च तदसाध्यं नेवम् अतिशब्देनात्र विशेषितत्वात् तेन तत्र मनाक्कृष्णत्वं वोध्यम् इति जेज्जटः अथवा जम्बूफलाभं यत् कृष्ण तदिति योज्यम । उक्तविकाराः श्वास-कासादयः । सुरपतिधनुषा तुल्यं नानावर्णम् । येनेत्यादि । येन रक्तपित्तेनेति योज्यम् । पश्येद्दृश्यं वियच्चापि अदृश्यमपि वियद्दृश्यमिव पश्यतीति योज्य रक्तपितोपहतनेत्रत्वादिति अथवा दृश्यं घटपटादि वियच्व रक्त पश्यतीति । अपरमसाध्यलक्षणमाह लोहितमित्यादि । यो बहुशश्छर्दयेदिति सम्बन्धः । लोहितोद्रारदर्शांति लोहितोद्रारो लोहितदशी च उन्नरोजप लोहितः प्रवर्तत इत्यर्थः अथवा लोहितमुद्गार पश्यतीति लोहितोद्गारदर्शीति ।।- इति श्रीविजयरक्षितकृतायां मध्यकोशव्याख्यायां रक्तपित्तनिदानं समाप्तम् ॥॥ - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
answer_text: the content This passage discusses the incurability of the raktapitta. The term kulhitam means putrefied and having bad smell. The term kardamambha refers to the dirty water mixed with soil. The term medahpityasrakalpam refers to the one that has the shape and colour of fat, pus, and blood. The term kalpa used here denotes a mixed shape involving a minor form of the above three substances of the blood discharged in the disease as emphasized upon by the scholar Gayadāsa. The term yakṛdiva means the one resembling (broken) liver in colour. The term pakvajabuphalam refers to the smoothness and blackness of a ripened fruit of Jambu. Likewise, the term surapatidhanusatulyam suggests a look resembling the rainbow or a mixture of various colours. The patient sees all things in red colour only as the term lohitodgāradarśī suggests. Thus concludes the Chapter on Raktapitta. MODERN PERSPECTIVES ON RAKTAPITTA OR PURPURA The modern science has identified a condition as purpura that could roughly identified with the disease raktapitta as is allegedly pro¬ duced from damage to the endotheliurn of small blood vessels, co¬ agulation defects, ineffective perivascular support, capillary fragility and permeability or a combination of these determinants. These faulty hemostatic determinants, in turn, can result from throm¬ bocylopenia or other hematologic disorders, invasive procedures and, of course, the application of anticoagulant drugs. Purpura (from Latin: purpura, meaning “purple”) is the appearance of red or purple discolorations on the skin that do not blanch on ap¬ plying pressure. They are caused by bleeding underneath the skin. Purpura measure 0.3-1 cm (3-10 mm). This is common with typhus and can be present with meningitis caused by meningococcal menin¬ gitis or septicaemia. In particular, meningococcus (Neisseria menin- gitidis), a Gram-negative diplococcus organism, releases endotox in when it lyses. Endotoxin activates the Hageman factor (clotting fac¬ tor XII), which causes disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The DIC is what appears as a rash on the affected individual. Purpura is the extravasations of red blood cells from the blood ves¬ sels into the skin, subcutaneous tissue, or mucous membranes. It is signified by discolouration—normally purplish or brownish red that is plainly visible through the epidermis. Purpuric lesions include petechiae, ecchymoses, and hematomas. Purpura differs from erythema in that it does not blanch with pressure because it involves blood in the tissues and not just dilated vessels. Additional causes are nonpathologic purpura can be a consequence of aging, when loss of collagen decreases connective tissue support of upper skin blood vessels. In the elderly or cachectic person, skin atrophy, inelasticity, and loss of subcutaneous fat promote suscep¬ tibility to minor trauma, causing purpura to appear along the veins of the forearms, hands, legs, and feet. Continued coughing or vomiting can generate crops of petechiae in loose face and neck tissue. Violent muscle contraction, as the one that occurs in seizures or weight lift- ing, sometimes occurs in localized ecchymoses from increased in¬ traluminal pressure and rupture. High fever, which advances capil¬ lary fragility, can also generate purpura. The sign of this disease could develop also due to following medical disorders: Amyloidoisis, autoerythrocyte sensitivity, dermatoses (pigmented), disseminated intravascular, coagulation, dysproteinemias, leasy bruising syndrome, ehlers-danlos syndrome (EDS), idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), leukemia, liver disease, lympho- mas, myeloproliferative disorders, nutritional deficiencies, septice- mia, stasis, systemic lupus erythematousus, thrombocytopenic pur- pura and trauma. The patient could be passed through certain diagnostic tests. These can include a peripheral blood smear, bone marrow test, and blood tests to ascertain platelet count, bleeding and coagulation times, cap- illary fragility, clot retraction, one-stage prothrombin time, activated partial thromho-plastin time and fibrinogen levels. The most common type of purpura in children is allergic purpura. Other causes in children include trauma, hemophilia, autoimmune hemolylic anemia, Citucher's disease, thrombasthenia, congenital determinant deficiencies, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, severe ITP, von Willehrand’s disease and the rare but life-threatening purpura, fulminans, which most normally follows bacterial or viral infection. Neonates normally manifest petechiae, particularly on the head, neck and shoulders, after vertex deliveries. These patches are thought to t result from the trauma of birth, they disappear within a few days. Other causes in infants include thrombocytopenia, vitamin K defi- ciency and infantile scurvy. As a child grows and tests his motor skills, the risk of accidents mul¬ tiplies and ecchyrnoses and hematomas normally occur. However, when the physician examines a child with purpura, he must be alert for symptoms of possible child abuse: bruises in different stages of resolution, from repeated beatings; bruise patterns resembling a fa- miliar object, such as a belt, hand or thumb and finger; and bruises on the face, buttocks or genital areas unlikely to be injured accidentally

पुरा लोमिनदैत्यानां निहतानां सुरैयुधि । उत्पन्नानि शरीरेभ्यो लोहानि विविधानि च । लोहोऽस्त्री शस्त्रकं तीक्ष्णं पिण्डं कालायसायसीः।।३९।।
answer_text: In ancient times when demon named Lolima was killed by devātas his blood drops fell on the earth which gave orgin to various types of Lohas. The Synonyms of Loha are: Śastraka, Tīkṣṇa, Piṇḍa, Kālāyaṣa and Ayasī. The word Loha is used in all gender expect feminine gender

explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Visa-Upavisa Varga, Chapter 7, verse 718.
context: पुरा लोमिनदैत्यानां निहतानां सुरैयुधि । उत्पन्नानि शरीरेभ्यो लोहानि विविधानि च । लोहोऽस्त्री शस्त्रकं तीक्ष्णं पिण्डं कालायसायसीः।।३९।।

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Ikshu Varga, Chapter 22, verse 1066):

इक्षो रसो यः सम्पक्को जायते लोष्टवद् दृढः । स गुडो, गौडदेशे तु मत्स्यण्ड्येव गुडो मतः ।।१४।। गुडो वृष्यो गुरुः स्निग्धो वातघ्नो मूत्रशोधनः । नातिपित्तहरो मेदःकफक्रिमिबलप्रदः ।। २५.।। गुडो जीर्णो लघुः पथ्योऽनभिष्यन्द्यग्निपुष्टिकृत् । पित्तघ्नो मधुरो वृष्यो वातघ्नोऽसुक्प्रसादनः ।। २६ ।। गुडो नवः कफश्वासक्रिमिकरोऽग्निकृत् । ! २७.।। श्लेष्माणमाशु विनिहन्ति सदार्ककेण पित्तं निहन्ति च तदेव हरीतकीभिः । शुण्ङ्ग्या समं हरति वातमशेषमित्यं दोषत्रयक्षयकराय नमो गुडाय ।। २८ ।।
answer_text: Sugarcane juice boiled till it becomes hard like a stone is called as Guḍa (Jaggery). In the gouda dēśa matśyandī is know as Guḍa. Guda is Vrṣya (Aphrodisiac), Guru (Heavy for digestion), Increases vāta dosa, Mūtraśhodaka (Clears the urine), Slightly increases Pitta dosa. It aggravates Medha (Fat), Kapha dosa, leads to Krmi (Worms infestations) and gives Bāla (Strength). Purana guḍa: Purana guḍa is Laghu (Light for digestion), Pathyā (Ideal diet), Abhiṣyanḍi (Blocks the channels), Agnikrt (Appetizer), Pustivardaka (Nutrient), Subsides pitta, Madhura (Sweet) in taste, Vrṣya (Aphrodisiac), Subsides vāta doṣa and Rakta prasādhana (Purifies the blood). Naveena guda: Naveena guda aggravates Kapha, leads to diseases like Swāsa (Dyspnoea) Kāsa (Cough), Kṛmi (Worm infestations) and acts as Agnikṛt (Appetizer). Properties of guda based on anupana: If Guḍa is consumed along with Adraka, it immediately destroyes kapha dosa, along with Harītakī it subsides pitta, with śuṇṭhī cures all vātagata rogas. So salutations to Guḍa which migrates all Tridosas
citation: Bhavaprakasha Nighantu — Ikshu Varga, Chapter 22, verse 1066
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Ikshu Varga, Chapter 22, verse 1066.
context: इक्षो रसो यः सम्पक्को जायते लोष्टवद् दृढः । स गुडो, गौडदेशे तु मत्स्यण्ड्येव गुडो मतः ।।१४।। गुडो वृष्यो गुरुः स्निग्धो वातघ्नो मूत्रशोधनः । नातिपित्तहरो मेदःकफक्रिमिबलप्रदः ।। २५.।। गुडो जीर्णो लघुः पथ्योऽनभिष्यन्द्यग्निपुष्टिकृत् । पित्तघ्नो मधुरो वृष्यो वातघ्नोऽसुक्प्रसादनः ।। २६ ।। गुडो नवः कफश्वासक्रिमिकरोऽग्निकृत् । ! २७.।। श्लेष्माणमाशु विनिहन्ति सदार्ककेण पित्तं निहन्ति च तदेव हरीतकीभिः । शुण्ङ्ग्या समं हरति वातमशेषमित्यं दोषत्रयक्षयकराय नमो गुडाय ।। २८ ।।

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Madhava Nidana (Laghutrayi) (Nidānasthāna, Chapter 31):

बस्तिकृण्डलमाह द्वतेत्यादि । लङ्कनमुत्सतनम् । उदृत्तः स्वस्थानादूध्वं गतः गर्भवदिति गर्भिण्या उदरान्तर्गतापत्यवत् एतेन बस्तिपुटस्य पार्श्वगमनं दर्शितम् । पीडित इति नाभेरधः । उद्वेष्टनार्तिः उद्वेष्टनरूपाऽऽर्तिः । शख्रविषोपमं शख्रविषसदृशमिति विभिन्नार्थि- सूचनार्थं प्रसिद्धानुभवोपदर्शनार्थम् ।। तस्मिन् पित्तान्विते दाहः शूलं मूत्रविवर्णता श्लेष्मणा गौरवं शोथः स्निग्धं मूत्रं घनं सितम् । वातस्यैव दोपान्तराहवन्धिनो लक्षणमाह तस्मिनित्यादि । श्लेष्मणा अन्विते तस्मिति बोड़व्यम् ।। -
answer_text: The above passage starting from the term druta etc., explains the nuances of the disease vastikundala. However, here too, the com¬ mentary mostly repeats the presentation of the original MN passage. Doşa - wise symptomatology of vasti kunḍala Condition of the colour of urine passed by the patient of vastikimdala changes if the condition has been complicated by different dosas. If there is vitiation of pitta dosa, the natural colour of urine is changed. The form of burning sensation and type of pain are also changed. If the disease is further complicated by vitiation of kapha the urine passed by patient gets thickened, smooth and its colour turns white. There is also feeling of heaviness and swelling in the lower abdomen. Here too, the commentary mostly repeats the presentation of the original MN passage without advancing or supplementing it
chapter_title: Mūtrāghāta Nidānam – Diagnosis of Urinary Obstruction
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Nidānasthāna, Chapter 31.

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Madhava Nidana (Laghutrayi) (Nidānasthāna, Chapter 12):

ऊर्ध्वश्वासलक्षणमाहऊर्ध्वमित्यादिना । ऊर्ध्वमिति विशेषपरं सर्वश्वासानां तथा- विधत्वात् । दीर्घमिति दीर्घकालम् । न च प्रत्याहारत्यध इति न श्वासमधः करोति दीर्घकाल- मित्यर्थः । श्लेष्मावृतमुखस्रोता इति श्लेष्मणा आवृतानि मुखं स्रोतांसि च यस्य स तथा । क्रुद्धगन्धवहादितः कुपितवातपीडितः समस्तपाठे तु श्लेष्मावृतमुखस्रोतस्त्वेन कुद्धो यो गन्धवहस्तेनार्दितः । विपश्यन् इतस्तत इति इतस्ततो विकृति पश्यन् । ऊध्वं श्वसिति यो दीर्घीन च प्रत्याहरत्यधः इति यदुक्तं तत्र हेतुमाह ऊर्ध्वश्वास इत्यादि । निरुध्यत इति हृदय एवांति- स्तम्भितः स्यात् अथवा श्वासो वातः सोऽधो न वर्तते । ऊध्वै श्वास ऊध्वधासः । ताम्यता ग्लायतो मुद्यतश्वासून् प्राणान् हन्ति नान्ययेति - यस्तु श्वसिति विच्छिन्नं सर्वप्राणेन पीडितः । श्वसिति दुःखार्तो मर्मच्छेदरुगर्दितः ॥॥ वा प दह्यमानेन का बस्तिना । अनाह-स्वेद-मूर्च्छार्तो - श्वसन् रक्तैकलोचनः विप्लुताक्षः परिक्षीणः विचेताः परिशुष्कास्यो विवर्णः प्रलपन्नरः । छिन्नश्वासेन विच्छिन्नः स शीघ्रं विजहात्यस्न् ॥ ॥ - - - - -
answer_text: The passage starting from urdhvam refers to the characteristics of the disease ūrdhvaśvāsa. Urdhva, which means upward breathing or breathing out heavily, is the symptom seen in all varieties of dyspnea. In the disease ūrdhvaśvāsa, however, exhalation takes comparatively a longer time than in a normal breathing. Thus, the patient has a delayed breathing-out. This morbid condition is produced due to kapha that chokes the respiratory channels. The term kruddhagan- dhavahārditah suggests that due to the vitiated vāta the patient faces a great trouble. It may be noted that the term śvāsa has been used to denote vāyu only. Other terms have been already explained in the above English translation. Chinna śvāsa (Interrupted dyspnoea) (CS. Ci. S. 17. 52-54) The fatal phase of the disease chinnasvasa is marked through the following features. The respiration is often interrupted in the middle, one feels a severe distress, one would not even attempt at respiration for fear of pain, and one has pain in all the vital organs. In that fatal stage, one’s abdomen is enlarged. There is heavy perspiration, faint- ing, burning sensation in one’s urinary bladder, whose eyes are filled with tears. One would suffer from emaciation, redness of one eye, loss of consciousness, severe dryness of the mouth, discolouration, delirium, looseness of all the joints and like symptoms when one has reached the fatal stage of the disease. Then one is understood to have reached an incurable stage of the disease chinnaśvāsa. 24–26
chapter_title: Hikkā Śvāsa Nidānam – Diagnosis of Hiccup and Dyspnoea
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Nidānasthāna, Chapter 12.

question:
Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Mamsa Varga, Chapter 10, verse 957):

हेमन्ते कूपजा मत्स्याः शिशिरे सारसा हिताः । वसन्ते तु नादेयाः ग्रीष्मे चौङ्यसमुद्धवाः ।। तडागजाता वर्षासु तास्वपथ्या नदी भवाः । नैझराः शरदि श्रेष्ठा विशेषोऽयमुदाहृतः ।।१२९।।
answer_text: Hemañta ṛtu (Durning winter): Fishes from the well are best. Śiśira ṛtu (Autumn season ): Fishes from the tributary of a river are ideal. Vasanta ṛtu (Spring season): Fishes collected from River are considered to be the best. Grīṣma ṛtu (Summer season): Fishes from the ponds are considered to be the best. Vraşā ṛtu ( Rainy seasons): Fishes from the lakes are preferred and durning same season fishes from river water should be avoided. Śarad ṛtu (Post rainy season): Fishes from the streams are perfect. 69 JA-413
citation: Bhavaprakasha Nighantu — Mamsa Varga, Chapter 10, verse 957
explanation: Answer as given by the commentary on Mamsa Varga, Chapter 10, verse 957.

Explain the meaning of the following verse from Bhavaprakasha Nighantu (Vari Varga, Chapter 12, verse 993):

पिच्छिलं कृमिलं क्लिन्न् पर्णशैवालकर्दमैः । विवर्णं विरसं सान्द्रं दुर्गन्थं न हित जलम् ।।७८।। कलुषं छन्नमम्भोजपर्णनीलीतृणादिभिः । दुःस्यर्शनमसंस्पृष्ट सौरचान्द्रमरीचिभिः ।।७९।। अनार्त्तवं वार्षिकं तु प्रथमं तच्च भूमिगम् । व्यापन्नं परिहर्तव्यं सर्वदोषप्रकोपणम् । ८.०।। तत्कुर्यात्स्रानपानाभ्यां तृष्णाऽऽध्मानचिरज्वरान् । कासाग्निमान्द्याभिष्यन्दकण्डूगण्डादिकं तथा ।।८११।।
answer_text: Water which is sticky, contaminated with worms, dried leaves, algea or mud, discolored, change in taste, thick, having foul odur is not good for consumption. question:

शाल्मलिस्तु भवेन्मोचा पिच्छिला पूरणीति च । रक्तपुष्पा स्थिरायुश्च कण्टकाढ्या च तूलिनी ।।५४।। शाल्मली शीतला स्वाद्वी रसे पाके रसायनी । श्लेष्मला पित्तवातास्वहारिणी रक्तपित्तजित् ।।५५।।
answer_text: Digestive disease: The bark exudation is very rich in Astringent useful in Atisāra (Diarrhea) and Pravāhika (Dysentery). In case of Krmi (Worm infestations), a paste prepared from seeds should be taken with Rice water or Butter milk. Respiratory diseases: A decoction of the bark is used in Kāsa (Cough) and Pinasa Common cold). Posionious bites: The bark is given with Śuṇṭhī in Sarpaviṣa (Snake bite). External uses: Paste prepared from Palāṣa Patra, Nimba or Badar with sour gruel applied locally to reduce Dāha (Burning sensation) in Jwara (Fever). The leaves are used externally in Vispoṭa (Blisters), Yavānpidika (Pimples), Vṛṇa (Wounds) etc 46 JA-413 In case of Vrścikāviṣa (Scorpion posion), Palāṣa seeds impregnated with Arka latex should be made into paste and applied locally. Mātrā (Part used): Bīja cūrna: 3-5gm, Patra swarasa: 10-20ml. Kwātha: 50-100ml. SĀLAMALI Latin: Bombax malabaricam DC. Fam: Malvaceae Hin: Salamali ng: Silk cotton tree Paryāyanāma (Synonyms): Śālmali, Mocā, Picchilā, Pūraṇi, Raktapuṣpā, Stirāyu, Kantakādhyā and Tūlinī. Guṇa karma (Properties and indications): It is Śīta vīrya (Cold in potency), Madhura vipāka (Sweet in taste), Rāsāyana (Rejuvenators), Increases Kapha, Subsides Pītta, Vāta and Rakta and cures Raktapitta (Haemorrages). Utpattisthāna (Natural territory): Commonly throughout india. Swarūpa (Botanical description): A large tree grows upto 40m. high. Leaves are palmate up to 50-60cm. long, 3-7 entire, leathery, smooth lanceolate to elliptic leaflets with pointed tips. The petioles are longer than the leaflets. Trunk straight, buttressed at the base, conical prickles on branches and especially on trunk Flowers are large 7.5cm. across, dark crimson, borne solitary or in clusters at the ends of the branches. Fruits are capsules reaches up to 15 cm. long, ovoid, pointed, embedded with white- silky cotton. Prayojya aṅga (Part used): Puṣpā (Flower), Niryasā (Gum), Twak (Bark). Chemical constituents: Gum exudates contains gallic and tannic acids. Flowers contain hentriacontane and gossypol. Root bark contains lupeol and β-D -glucoside

अवबाहुकमाह सिराधेत्यादिना । तत्रस्थोंऽसदेशस्थः सिरा आकुञ्यावबाहुकं जनयेत् । अयं वात-कफजः । अन्ये तु मिलित्वाऽवबाहुकलक्षणमाहुः तन्न यतः सुश्रुतेनो- क्तम- अंसशोषावबाहकयोर्बाहमध्ये सिराव्यधः सु०शा० इति । एतदनन्तरं सुश्रतेन बाधियं पठितं - यदा शब्दवहं वायुः सुनि इत्यादिना माधवेन तु प्रकरणानुरोधं मन्यमानेन कर्णरोग एव तत् पठितं किन्तु सुश्रुतेन् वातव्याधौ बाधियं पठित्वाऽपि बाधिर्यकर्णशूलौ शालाक्येऽपि पंठितो पुनरुक्तमिति चेत् न सम्प्राप्तिभेदभिन्नत्वात वातव्याधौ शब्दवहमित्यनेन कर्णशष्कुल्यवच्छिन्ननभोदेश उक्तः शालाक्ये च शब्दवहाः सिरा इत्युक्तम् । माधवेन तु कर्णरोगे शब्दाश्रवणत्वाविशेषादेतदेव तत्र पठितमित्यविरोधः ।। आवृत्य वायुः सकफो धमनीः शब्दवाहिनीः ॥॥ नरान् करोत्यक्रियकान्मूक-मिन्मिन-गद्नदान । - -

Ni. 1.85) The vāta getting provoked along with kapha moves to the dhamanīs of the vocal cord and subsequently turn the person unable to talk or make him talk through his nose. context: दन्तनिष्यीडितस्येक्षो रसः पित्तास्त्रनाशनः । शर्करासमवीर्यः स्यादविदाही कफप्रदः ।।१६।। मूलाग्रजन्तुग्रन्थ्यादिपीडनान्मलसङ्कराद् किश्चित्कालविधृत्या च विकृतिं याति यान्त्रिकः ।। तस्माद्विदाही विष्टम्भी गुरुः स्याद्यान्त्रिको रसः ।।१७।। रसः पर्युषितो नेष्टो ह्यम्लो वातापहो गुरुः । कफपित्तकरः शोषी भेदनश्चातिमूत्रलः ।।१८।। पक्को रसो गुरुः स्निग्याः सुतीक्ष्णः कफवातनुत् । गुल्मानाहप्रशमनः किश्चित्पित्तकरः स्मृतः ।।१९५४ इक्षोर्विकारास्तृड्दाहमूर्व्छापित्तास्त्रनाशनाः गुरवो मधुरा बल्याः स्निग्धा वातहराः सराः । वृष्यमोहहराः शीता वृंहणा विषहारिणीः ।।२० ।। इक्षो रसस्तु यः पक्कः किश्चिद्राढो बहुद्रवः । स एवेक्षुविकोरेषु ख्यातः फणितसंज्ञया । फााणित गुर्वभिष्यन्दि बृहण कफशुक्रकृत् । वातपित्तश्रमान्हन्ति मूत्रवस्तिविशोधनम् । । २ १ । । इक्षो रसो यः सम्पक्को घनः किश्चिद् द्रवान्वितः । मन्दे यत्-दते तस्मात्तन्मत्स्यण्डी निगद्यते ।।२२।। मत्स्यण्डी भेदिनी बल्या लघ्वी पित्तानिलापहा । मधुरा बृंहणी वृष्या रक्तदोषापहा स्मृता ।।२३।।
